name: Fragrance pyramid (top/heart/base notes)

lead: The fragrance pyramid splits a perfume into top (head) notes, heart (middle) notes and base notes, in order of how quickly they evaporate. Top notes such as citrus, mint or lavender are perceived first, heart notes form the main body, and base notes like amber, musk or tobacco give depth and last longest.

For appearance it is a tool for choosing a scent: knowing the stages helps someone judge how a fragrance will smell on arrival and at the end of the day, which affects the impression they leave. Brands often print the pyramid on packaging and product pages.

paras: People sample a fragrance on skin and wait through the stages before choosing, often reading note lists. Concentrations such as eau de toilette or eau de parfum also affect how long the stages last.
Fragrance is low risk for most people, though some experience skin irritation or allergic reactions to ingredients, and strong scents can bother others.

angle.text: Choosing a scent with the pyramid in mind helps someone smell pleasant from the first spray through the dry-down, which contributes to overall grooming and impression.

lead: The fragrance pyramid is a framework that describes a perfume as three groups of notes released in sequence. Top (head) notes are small, light molecules that evaporate quickly and shape the first impression; middle (heart) notes emerge as the top fades and form the main body; base notes appear later and provide depth and longevity.[1]

People use it to understand how a scent will change on skin and to choose fragrances that suit different settings. Manufacturers frequently present notes as a pyramid, often using imaginative rather than technical labels.[1]

Concentration also shapes the experience: parfum or extrait is typically 15 to 30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum about 15 to 20%, eau de toilette 5 to 15% and cologne 2 to 3%, though houses vary.[1] The framework is descriptive and used in the trade and consumer education rather than a chemical classification.
infobox: Fast evaporating; e.g. citrus, mint, lavender[1]

paras: Top notes are noticed immediately after application. Heart notes appear as these fade and partly mask the sometimes unpleasant early smell of base notes. Base notes show after roughly half an hour and linger. The layers interact: base notes influence how the top and heart are perceived, and heart notes can alter the base.[1]
General guides give approximate wear times of about two hours for cologne, two to four for eau de toilette and up to six to eight for perfume, with house-to-house variation.[1]

No studies found on the pyramid as a framework. Related research includes work on how aldehydes such as nonanal and decanal, used to enhance floral and citrus notes, affect human brain electrical activity depending on the nostril sniffed.[2]

timeline.event: Guerlain's Jicky is an early perfume with a high concentration of aromatics.[1]
Eau de parfum appears and becomes widespread in the 1980s.[1]
